The two solvent-recovery papers, one by Bai et al. and the other by Essehli et al., use different approaches to recover the PVDF binder. Bai et al. use a Cyrene-based separation process, where the PVDF binder is dissolved in Cyrene at high temperatures (around 100°C) and then separated from the cathode materials through a combination of centrifugation, filtration, and phase separation. The recovered PVDF binder is then reused, and the process is repeated to achieve a closed-loop recycling process.

In contrast, Essehli et al. use an ethylene glycol (EG)-based separation process, where the PVDF binder is dissolved in EG at high temperatures (around 160°C) and then separated from the cathode materials through a combination of centrifugation, filtration, and screen filtration. The recovered PVDF binder is then washed and dried to remove any residual EG.

Both processes involve the use of a solvent to dissolve the PVDF binder, but the specific approach and conditions used differ between the two studies.
